---
title: "Quiz: choosing the threshold from the histogram"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Class 0 is background ($i \le t$), class 1 is object; $\omega_k$, $\mu_k$, $\sigma_k^2$ are the class weights, means and variances.

---

**Q1.** Why is minimising the within-class variance the same as maximising the between-class variance?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to the total variance when $t$ moves?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Total = within + between, and the total variance of all pixels does not depend on $t$. Whatever the within part loses, the between part gains.
:::

---

**Q2.** Two splits have class means 40 and 200. In split A the classes hold 50 % and 50 % of the pixels; in split B 99 % and 1 %. Which has the larger $\sigma_B^2$, and by how much?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\sigma_B^2 = \omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A: $0.25 \cdot 160^2 = 6400$. B: $0.0099 \cdot 160^2 = 253$. A is about 25 times larger: Otsu prefers splits where both classes are substantial.
:::

---

**Q3.** One isodata step: the current split has class means 60 and 140. Where does the threshold go next? When does isodata stop?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Midpoint.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
To $(60 + 140)/2 = 100$. It stops when the new midpoint gives the same split as before: every pixel is then nearer to its own class mean (a fixed point, as in k-means with $k = 2$).
:::

---

**Q4.** Objects are rare (5 % of the pixels) and both classes have the same spread. Is the minimum-error threshold above or below the midpoint of the two means?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
At the midpoint, which class is more likely for a pixel?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Above (towards the object mean). At the midpoint both densities are equal, but background is 19 times more common, so a pixel there is probably background. The boundary moves towards the rarer class until the weighted densities are equal.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why can the minimum-error rule with unequal variances label a pixel **object** when it is darker than the background mean?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare the tails of a narrow and a wide normal curve.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
If the object class is much wider, its density decays more slowly than the narrow background peak, so far below the background mean the object density is larger again. The weighted curves cross twice, and the Bayes rule says "object" in both tails. (In practice that dark tail holds very few pixels.)
:::

---

**Q6.** A fluorescence image has a huge dark background peak and a faint tail of a few bright spots, with no valley. Which method would you try first, and why does Otsu fail?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Otsu needs both classes to be substantial.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The triangle method (or maximum entropy): it is made for a unimodal histogram with a long tail and puts $t$ where the peak ends. Otsu's $\sigma_B^2$ barely rewards separating a 1 % class, so it splits the background peak instead.
:::

---

**Q7.** Two classes overlap so much that the best possible threshold misclassifies 20 % of the pixels. Will a cleverer histogram method do better?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What information does any histogram method use?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. The Bayes threshold is already the best rule that looks at one grey level at a time. To do better you need more information than the grey level of a single pixel: its neighbours (smoothing, graph cuts) or other features.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that $\mu_0 - \mu = \omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1)$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\mu = \omega_0\mu_0 + \omega_1\mu_1$ and $\omega_0 = 1 - \omega_1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\mu_0 - \mu = \mu_0 - (1 - \omega_1)\mu_0 - \omega_1\mu_1 = \omega_1\mu_0 - \omega_1\mu_1 = \omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1)$.
:::
